title: Evals in production
summary: How to test a system built on a language model: a set of cases, graders that score the outputs, a check before every change, and a sample of real traffic after.

blocks.p: You change a prompt to fix one bad answer. It works for that case. Did it break ten others? A model's output varies from run to run, and an exact-match test fails good answers that are worded differently.
Without a way to measure, every change is a guess, and switching to a new model is a leap of faith.

An **eval** runs the system on a fixed set of cases and scores each output. It plays the part tests play in other code. Run it before every change to prompts, models, tools or retrieval, and compare the score with the current version.

Each case is an input and what a good output must do. Start with real requests, especially ones that went wrong. A few dozen cases that cover the important kinds of request beat thousands of made-up ones.

list: **Code checks.** Exact facts, valid JSON, the right tool called, a link present, a length limit. Fast, cheap and repeatable. Use them wherever they fit.

**A model as judge.** Another model scores the output against a written rubric, such as "answers only from the given sources". It handles qualities code can't check. Test it against human labels before trusting it.
**People.** Domain experts review a sample. Slow and costly, but they set the standard the other graders are checked against.

blocks.caption: Before shipping, a change runs against the case set and is compared with the current version. In production, a sample of real traffic is graded, and failures become new cases.

blocks.p: A score from a small set is noisy. With 40 of 50 cases passing, the true rate could plausibly be anywhere from about 67% to 89%. A change from 40 to 42 passes tells you almost nothing.

blocks.caption: The range of true pass rates that fit what you measured, from the number of cases and how many passed. It uses the Wilson interval, which stays between 0% and 100% even with few cases.

blocks.p: To compare two versions, run both on the same cases and count the cases that changed: fixed by the new version, and broken by it. Cases both versions pass or both fail say nothing about the difference. If 25 cases were fixed and 7 broken, the new version is ahead by 18. With only 3 fixed and 1 broken, the difference could easily be chance. The Anthropic paper below shows how to put error bars on this paired difference.

Real users ask things your case set doesn't cover. Log every request with its trace, as in the observability lesson. Grade a sample every day with the same graders, and watch the pass rate like any other metric. Read the failures, and add the instructive ones to the case set.

list: **Model judges agree with people about as often as people agree with each other.** [Zheng and others](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685) found that strong models as judges matched human preferences over 80% of the time. They also found biases toward the first answer shown and toward longer answers.

**Report error bars.** Anthropic's [A statistical approach to model evaluations](https://www.anthropic.com/research/statistical-approach-to-model-evals) recommends reporting the standard error with every eval score, and comparing two models question by question.

**Look at the data.** Hamel Husain's [Your AI Product Needs Evals](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals/) argues for reading many real traces before writing graders, and for building evals step by step.
**Keep the set fresh.** A case set that never changes stops catching new failures. Add cases from production, and keep a few that the system still fails.
An eval runs the system on a fixed set of cases and scores each output.
Use code checks where you can, a model judge where you must, and people to check both.
Small sets give noisy scores, so check the margin of error before trusting a difference.
Grade a sample of production traffic, and turn failures into new cases.

rows.label: Lowest plausible true rate (%)
rows.expr: (() => { const q = k / n, z = 1.96; return Math.max(0, (q + z * z / (2 * n) - z * Math.sqrt(q * (1 - q) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n))) / (1 + z * z / n) * 100); })()

rows.label: Highest plausible true rate (%)
rows.expr: (() => { const q = k / n, z = 1.96; return Math.min(100, (q + z * z / (2 * n) + z * Math.sqrt(q * (1 - q) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n))) / (1 + z * z / n) * 100); })()
